page: Amazon Web Services x8g.4xlarge is a memory-optimized instance running on the AWS Nitro hypervisor. The instance is powered by an arm64-based AWS Neoverse-V2 processor clocked at 2.8 GHz, delivering 16 dedicated physical cores and 16 vCPUs without simultaneous multithreading. It features 64 KB of L1 data cache, 2 MB of L2 cache, and 36 MB of shared L3 cache. Memory density is the defining architectural metric of this configuration, offering 256.0 GB of RAM, which equates to an extensive 16.0 GB of memory per core. Local storage is not provided, requiring external network-attached storage, and baseline network bandwidth is set to 8 Gbps. There are no onboard GPUs.

Benchmark outcomes demonstrate clear alignment with memory-centric workloads. In synthetic memory testing, the instance achieved a top-tier PassMark memory score of 3,097.48 points, supported by strong uncached memory bandwidth of 292.71 GB/sec for 256 MB reads and 124.24 GB/sec for writes. PassMark database operations also performed well within the upper 25th percentile with 23,817.9 points, alongside solid Redis throughput at 32.54 million SET operations per second. General CPU compute benchmarks, including Geekbench (1,877.0 single-core, 15,801.0 multi-core) and Stress-NG, fell predominantly into the middle 50% percentile. Without hardware accelerators, text generation and LLM prompt processing exhibit notable performance limitations, recording poor figures on smaller models (18.4 tokens/sec on 135M text generation).

Because the Neoverse-V2 cores achieve consistent 1:1 physical-to-virtual CPU mapping without hyperthreading contention, the server delivers predictable performance for workloads bound by memory capacity rather than raw compute cycles. The qualitative cost efficiency is centered entirely on its 16:1 RAM-to-vCPU ratio, which reduces the need to over-provision compute cores merely to satisfy memory footprints. The absence of local NVMe storage and discrete GPUs is an intentional tradeoff, tailoring the instance specifically toward in-memory caching platforms, distributed key-value datastores, enterprise memory-bound databases, and large-footprint analytical batch processes.
